messages.content:
Explain to a second-year beekeeper why a colony swarms and which signs show up in the fortnight beforehand.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.

A colony swarms because it is reproducing at the colony level. The old queen leaves with a large group of workers to start a new nest, while the remaining bees raise a new queen in the original hive. It is usually a sign that the colony has become strong enough to divide, rather than simply a sign that something has gone wrong.

Swarming is encouraged by a combination of a rapidly growing population, plentiful nectar and pollen, an ageing or less productive queen, restricted space for brood rearing, and limited space for bees to cluster inside the hive. Congestion matters, but adding an empty box alone does not always stop a colony that has already committed to swarming. The bees are responding to their overall conditions, including the amount of open brood, the queen’s pheromones being spread through a very large population, and the availability of suitable queen-cell sites.

In the fortnight before a prime swarm, the colony often becomes exceptionally busy and crowded. Frames may be covered with bees, and the brood nest may be packed with emerging young bees. You may see many drones, especially at the edges or lower parts of brood frames, because a colony preparing to raise a new queen needs drones available for mating. Drone brood alone is not proof of swarming, but heavy drone production alongside other signs is significant.

The most useful early sign is the appearance of queen cups, usually along the lower edges of brood comb. Empty dry cups are common and are not, by themselves, evidence that the colony will swarm. Concern begins when you find an egg or a young larva in a cup and the bees have started drawing it out into a proper queen cell. These are often called charged queen cells. In a swarm-preparation situation, there may be several of them, commonly along the lower edges of frames, although location is not an absolute rule.

Once queen cells are being fed royal jelly and extended, the colony may already be well advanced in its preparations. The workers often begin reducing the old queen’s egg laying. This both creates room and helps make her lighter and more able to fly. You may notice less fresh brood than expected for a colony of that size, patchier egg laying, or brood frames being filled with nectar around the edges and in cells that would otherwise be available for eggs. This is called backfilling of the brood nest and is a strong warning sign when combined with charged swarm cells.

The queen may look slimmer, and workers may seem less intent on feeding or attending her than usual. She can still be present and laying, so finding the queen does not mean the colony is safe from swarming. A colony can swarm with the old queen very soon after you have seen her.

Bees may gather at the entrance, hang in a beard on the outside of the hive, or appear to have little room to move between frames. These signs can also be caused by hot weather or poor ventilation, so they should not be used alone as evidence of swarm preparation. Likewise, a sudden change in temperament is unreliable. Some colonies become more active and restless before swarming, while others remain calm.

Timing is important. A queen cell is usually capped about eight days after the egg is laid. Many colonies leave with the prime swarm around the time the first swarm cells are capped, though they can go earlier or later depending on weather and colony conditions. Therefore, if you find charged swarm cells containing larvae and royal jelly, you should assume the colony may swarm within days rather than waiting until the next routine inspection.

A swarm pattern is usually different from supersedure or emergency queen replacement. Swarm preparation often involves numerous queen cells, a very strong crowded colony, abundant brood and bees, and cells around the lower frame edges. Supersedure more often involves a smaller number of queen cells, sometimes on the face of the comb, while the colony is trying to replace an ageing or failing queen without dividing. Emergency cells appear after a queen has been lost or damaged and are often made from existing worker larvae, scattered over the brood area.

The practical lesson is to inspect strong colonies frequently during swarm season, often every seven days, and look especially for charged queen cells, not merely empty cups. Once proper swarm cells are present, simply cutting them out usually delays rather than solves the problem, because the colony may rebuild them or swarm anyway. A proper swarm-control method that creates the conditions the bees were seeking is generally more reliable.

scenario.task: Explain to a second-year beekeeper why a colony swarms and which signs show up in the fortnight beforehand.

Explain to a first-time exhibitor how to price work for a craft fair without either underselling or pricing for nobody.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use any of these words: important, significant.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use quotation marks.

Start by finding your minimum sustainable price, then compare it with what shoppers at that fair are likely to pay. Good pricing sits where those two realities overlap.

Your minimum price needs to cover more than raw materials. Include the materials used in one piece, packaging, your labor, a share of studio costs, the booth fee, travel, card-processing fees, and a profit margin for the business. Your labor should be paid at an hourly rate you can live with, not treated as free because you enjoy making the work.

For example, imagine a piece uses $12 in materials and takes 1.5 hours to make. If you pay yourself $20 per hour, labor is $30. Add $8 for packaging and general overhead, plus $10 as that piece’s share of the event costs. Your base cost is now $60. If card fees and other selling costs take about 8 percent, and you want some profit beyond your wage, a retail price around $80 to $90 may be more realistic than $60.

The booth fee should be spread across the number of items you reasonably expect to sell, not every item you bring. If a weekend booth costs $300 and you expect to sell 30 pieces, each sold piece needs to contribute about $10 toward that fee. If you sell fewer pieces, the fair becomes less profitable, so estimate conservatively.

Then study the event before deciding whether your calculated price fits. Look at the fair’s website, vendor photos, social media, admission price, location, and past attendance. A juried indoor art market, a neighborhood street fair, and a holiday school bazaar may attract very different spending habits. Find makers whose work is comparable in materials, skill, scale, and finish. Do not compare your handmade ceramic mug with mass-produced mugs, and do not copy the price of a maker with a much more established following or lower production costs.

If your sustainable price is higher than the apparent market range, do not automatically cut it. First ask whether the fair is the right venue, whether your work is being presented clearly enough, or whether you need products at several price levels. A table with only $200 pieces may struggle at a casual fair, while a table with only $10 items may make it hard to cover a costly booth.

A healthy display often offers an entry point, a core range, and a few higher-priced pieces. The entry pieces let new customers try your work. The core range is where many sales may happen. The higher-priced work shows the depth of your skill and can raise the perceived value of everything else. Each item still needs to make financial sense; cheap items that take too long can quietly drain your time.

Price consistently. If two pieces take similar time and use similar materials, their prices should make sense together. Customers notice when a larger or more detailed piece costs barely more than a simpler one. Clear size-based or complexity-based pricing also makes it easier to answer questions at the booth without hesitation.

Avoid pricing only from emotion. A price based on guilt, fear of losing a sale, or embarrassment about charging for labor usually leads to underselling. On the other hand, a high price needs support from craftsmanship, presentation, materials, story, and a fair whose customers can afford it. Clean displays, readable signs, polished packaging, and clear descriptions help buyers understand why the work costs what it does.

Use the first few fairs as research. Track what sells, what gets picked up but not bought, what customers ask about, your average sale, and whether you covered the full cost of attending. If many people buy easily and you sell out early, your prices may be too low. If people admire the work but consistently hesitate at the same price point, try improving the presentation, offering a smaller version, or testing a modest adjustment rather than slashing every price.

Finally, do not forget sales tax. Decide whether it is included in the displayed price or added at checkout, follow local rules, and keep records. A price is only successful if it pays you, pays the event costs, fits the audience, and leaves you wanting to make the work again.

scenario.task: Explain to a first-time exhibitor how to price work for a craft fair without either underselling or pricing for nobody.

Explain to a new driver how to get a car moving on an icy incline without spinning the wheels, and when to give up and walk. These requirements came off a template, so use your judgement. The finished piece reading well matters more than ticking every one.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use any of these phrases: as an ai, large language model.
Do not use the letter a anywhere in your response, including inside words.
Do not use any of these words: snow, winter.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.

Icy Hill: Getting Moving

On ice, use smooth, tiny inputs. Keep tires pointed uphill. If you get level room before the rise, build only slight speed; do not gun it.

Use second, if your vehicle offers it, or use low-grip mode. Less drive force helps tires hold. In stick shift, lift clutch slowly while using only tiny throttle. In self-shift, let idle move you, if it will.

If tires spin, lift off throttle right off. Let tires grip once more, then retry with even less force. Do not pump throttle or flick wheel from side to side. Gentle, slow motion gives you best odds.

Stop trying if spin keeps coming, if your vehicle slips sidewise, if you lose uphill motion, or if it needs more force to keep moving. Spinning will slick ice still more.

Pull off only where you find room well off routes used by others. Turn on emergency lights. Get out only if footing is firm; keep well off routes.

If no secure pull-off spot exists, sit inside, lock doors, use your phone, then get tow help. Go on foot only if moving vehicles pose no risk, footing is firm, clothing is fit for cold, plus help or shelter is close by.

Explain to somebody renewing a passport why the photograph keeps being rejected and how to get one that will pass.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use any of these words: actually, basically.
Do not use any of these phrases: in conclusion, to sum up.

Passport photographs are often rejected because they are checked by both software and a human reviewer. The image must make it easy to confirm your identity and must meet strict technical rules. A photo can look good to you yet still fail because of lighting, cropping, image quality, or facial expression.

Common reasons for rejection include:

- Shadows on the face or behind the head
- A background that is not plain, light, and evenly lit
- Smiling, raised eyebrows, open mouth, or an expression that changes your usual appearance
- Hair covering the eyes, eyebrows, or too much of the face
- Glasses causing glare, dark lenses, tinted lenses, or frames obscuring the eyes
- Head too large, too small, too high, or too low in the frame
- Head tilted, turned, or not facing directly forward
- Poor focus, low resolution, blur, grain, or heavy compression
- Filters, skin smoothing, red-eye correction, altered colours, or other editing
- A photo that is too old or no longer reflects your current appearance
- Incorrect print size, digital dimensions, or file format
- A photo taken too close to a wall, creating a shadow
- Clothing blending into the background
- A child, hand, chair, toy, or another person visible in the image

To get a photo that is likely to pass:

1. Use a professional passport photo service if possible. Tell them it is for a passport renewal and name the country issuing the passport, since requirements differ.

2. If taking it yourself, stand in front of a plain light-coloured wall with even daylight or soft lighting from both sides. Avoid direct flash and overhead lighting.

3. Face the camera straight on. Keep your head level, look directly into the lens, keep both eyes open, and use a neutral expression with your mouth closed.

4. Keep hair away from your eyes and face. If you wear a religious or medical head covering, ensure your full face is visible from the bottom of your chin to the top of your forehead.

5. Remove glasses unless there is a medical reason not to. If glasses must be worn, make sure there is no glare and that the frames do not cover any part of the eyes.

6. Do not use portrait mode, beauty mode, filters, retouching, or background replacement tools. These are frequent causes of digital rejection.

7. Use a sharp, high-resolution image. The camera should be at eye level, and the photo should be taken against a stable background.

8. Follow the official size and cropping guide exactly. Pay close attention to required head size and the amount of space above the head.

9. Use the passport office online photo checker before submitting, if one is available. It can catch many technical problems before you send the application.

10. If the photo has already been rejected more than once, use an approved in-person photo provider rather than attempting another home photo. Bring or show the official photo rules so the provider can match them precisely.

The safest approach is a recent, unedited, sharply focused image with a neutral expression, plain evenly lit background, no shadows, and precise official cropping.

scenario.task: Explain to somebody renewing a passport why the photograph keeps being rejected and how to get one that will pass.

Explain to a beginner why their night-sky exposures come out with streaked stars, and the two fixes that cost nothing. If any requirement gets in the way of a clear answer, the requirement loses. We would rather have something usable.

Sky lights make lines in long shots as we spin. As we spin, each light shifts on the imaging chip while the shot is being made.

A second no-cost fix is to make lots of quick shots, then stack them with a no-cost app. The app adds the light but keeps each dot small.

Explain to somebody starting rotating shifts why a dark, cool room matters more than the number of hours they manage to get. Previous drafts followed the brief to the letter and read like a form. Loosen whichever rule is doing the damage.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use any of these words: sleep, nap, naps.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.

With rotating shifts, the number on the clock can be misleading. Eight hours in a bright, warm room with daylight leaking in may leave you more drained than six solid hours in a dark, cool, quiet one.

Your body clock still treats light as a signal to be alert. If you are trying to rest after a night shift while the room is bright, your brain gets mixed messages: it is tired, but the environment is saying daytime and activity. Darkness helps reduce that conflict and lets your body settle into deeper, less interrupted rest.

Temperature matters for the same reason. The body naturally cools down during its main recovery period. A stuffy or overheated room can cause more tossing, brief awakenings, and lighter rest, even if you never fully notice them. A cool room makes it easier to stay settled.

So do not judge recovery only by hours spent in bed. Start by making the room as dark, cool, and quiet as you can: blackout curtains or an eye mask, a fan or cooler air, and a plan to reduce interruptions. Once the environment is working with your body rather than against it, the hours you do get tend to count for more.

messages.content:
Explain to a first-time exhibitor how to price work for a craft fair without either underselling or pricing for nobody.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use any of these words: thing, things, stuff.

Start with a price based on your real costs, not just what feels affordable to customers. Add up materials, packaging, labels, payment-processing fees, booth fees, travel, insurance, tools, studio expenses, and a reasonable allowance for waste or mistakes. Then pay yourself for the time involved, including design, preparation, making, finishing, packing, and selling.

A simple starting formula is:

Materials and direct costs + labor + share of business expenses + profit = retail price

For labor, choose an hourly rate that respects your skill and experience. A newer maker might begin at a modest local wage, while a highly skilled or specialized maker should charge more. If a piece takes three hours and you want to earn $20 per hour, labor alone is $60 before materials or overhead.

Booth fees deserve special attention. If your booth costs $200 and you expect to sell 20 pieces, each piece needs to contribute about $10 toward that fee. If you expect to sell only 10 pieces, the share rises to $20 each. Do not let event costs quietly erase your earnings.

Next, compare your prices with comparable work in your area and at similar fairs. Look for makers with a similar level of skill, materials, size, finish, and customer base. You do not need to match every nearby price, but you should understand the local range. If your calculated price is far above comparable work, ask whether your process is inefficient, your labor rate needs gradual adjustment, or your work needs stronger presentation and a clearer reason for its value. If your calculated price is far below comparable work, raise it. Low prices can make customers question quality and can make it difficult to sustain your business.

Offer a range of prices so visitors have more than one way to buy. Include a few accessible options that introduce people to your work, a core selection that represents your usual price level, and a small number of larger or more detailed pieces. This helps avoid relying entirely on low-cost sales while still welcoming customers who are discovering your work for the first time.

Presentation supports price. Clean displays, clear signage, good packaging, consistent branding, and concise descriptions of materials and process all help customers understand why your work costs what it does. A handmade ceramic mug, print, textile piece, or piece of jewelry is not priced only for its raw materials; it also reflects design, skill, time, originality, and the experience of buying directly from the maker.

At your first fair, treat pricing as a test rather than a permanent decision. Track what sells, what gets picked up but not purchased, what customers ask about, and which price points move fastest. If nearly everything sells early, especially your higher-priced work, you may be priced too low. If people respond warmly but rarely buy, review whether the price, display, audience, or product mix needs adjustment. Change prices gradually rather than making dramatic swings after one event.

Avoid discounting just because sales are slow. A small, clearly planned offer, such as a bundle price or an end-of-show promotion, can work, but constant bargaining teaches customers to wait for reductions. It is usually better to make a smaller version, a simpler design, or a lower-cost edition than to cut the price of work that already needs to cover your costs.

The goal is not to be the cheapest booth or the most expensive booth. The goal is a price that pays you fairly, covers the cost of participating, fits the quality and market position of your work, and gives customers a believable reason to buy.

scenario.task: Explain to a first-time exhibitor how to price work for a craft fair without either underselling or pricing for nobody.

Explain to a first-time landlord what an inventory is for, who should hold it, and what makes one worthless in a dispute. If any requirement gets in the way of a clear answer, the requirement loses. We would rather have something usable.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use any of these phrases: a wide range of, a variety of.

An inventory is the record of the property’s condition and contents at the start of a tenancy. Its main job is to show what was there, what condition it was in, and whether anything was already damaged, worn, stained, missing or dirty before the tenant moved in.

It is used again when the tenant leaves. The check-out report is compared with the check-in inventory to decide whether the tenant has caused damage or left the property in a worse condition than at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. Without a good inventory, it can be very difficult for a landlord to justify deductions from a tenant’s deposit.

The landlord or managing agent should keep the original signed inventory and all supporting evidence, such as dated photographs, video, invoices and check-in/check-out reports. The tenant should be given a complete copy promptly and should have a reasonable opportunity to point out errors or add comments. Ideally, both landlord or agent and tenant sign and date it, or there is clear evidence that the tenant received it and had the chance to respond.

An inventory becomes weak, and may be effectively worthless in a deposit dispute, if it cannot reliably prove the property’s starting condition. Common problems include an inventory that is vague, undated, unsigned, not given to the tenant, completed after the tenant moved in, or missing photographs. Descriptions such as “good condition” or “clean” are often too vague on their own. It is better to record details, such as “small chip to rim of bathroom sink,” “two thumb-sized marks on living-room wall beside window,” or “oven greasy, particularly on inner glass and trays.”

Poor-quality photos can also undermine it. Photos should be clear, dated or otherwise traceable to the inspection, and wide enough to identify the room as well as close enough to show the issue. A photograph of a stain without showing where it is in the property may not prove much.

An inventory is also weak if the check-out inspection is not done fairly or if it compares different standards. For example, a landlord cannot claim for replacing an old carpet just because it has become more worn through normal use. The tenant is usually responsible for damage beyond fair wear and tear, not for improving the landlord’s property or paying new-for-old replacement costs.

The strongest approach is an independent professional inventory clerk, a detailed check-in report completed immediately before or at move-in, clear dated photographs, tenant acknowledgement and comments, and an equally detailed check-out report. If there is a dispute, the evidence must show not merely that the property is worse at the end, but what it was like at the beginning and why the tenant is responsible.

Explain to somebody who has just moved to the city how a contactless daily cap works and why tapping out at the end still matters.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use any of these phrases: on the other hand, that being said.
Do not use any of these words: train, trains, subway, rail.

A contactless daily cap is the maximum you will pay for eligible travel in one day when you use the same contactless card or mobile device.

Here’s how it works:

- Tap in at the start of each journey and tap out at the end.
- Each journey is charged normally at first.
- Once your total reaches the day’s cap, further eligible journeys that day cost nothing extra.
- The cap usually applies only within a set area, time period, and group of services, so check the local operator’s rules.
- Use the exact same card or phone every time. A physical card and that card added to a phone are often treated as two separate payment methods.

Tapping out still matters because it tells the system where your journey ended. Without it, the system may not know which fare applies and can charge an incomplete-journey or maximum fare. That extra charge may not count toward the cap in the same way, and it can make your travel history harder to correct.

In short: the cap protects you from paying beyond a daily limit, while tapping out makes sure each journey is priced correctly.

scenario.task: Explain to somebody who has just moved to the city how a contactless daily cap works and why tapping out at the end still matters.

A reserves policy is an agreed plan for how much money the charity should keep available, why it needs that amount, and how trustees will review it. Reserves are usually unrestricted funds that can be used for the charity’s general purposes. They are different from money held for a specific donor-funded purpose, such as restricted funds, because those funds cannot normally cover other costs.

For a small charity, reserves can provide a cushion when income arrives late, a grant ends, fundraising is weaker than expected, or an unexpected cost arises. They can also allow the charity to plan responsibly, meet commitments to staff and suppliers, and avoid stopping services abruptly.

The policy should reflect the charity’s own circumstances rather than an arbitrary target. Trustees might consider regular running costs, reliance on a small number of income sources, likely timing gaps between income and expenditure, financial risks, commitments already made, and any planned future spending. It should also explain when reserves may be used and how they will be rebuilt afterwards.

The regulator asks because trustees have a duty to manage charity money prudently and to protect the charity’s ability to carry out its purposes. A policy shows that the trustees have considered financial resilience rather than accumulating funds without a reason or leaving the charity exposed by holding too little. It also helps supporters, funders, and beneficiaries understand why the charity holds money instead of spending all of it immediately.

The policy need not be long or complicated. What matters is that it is evidence-based, approved by the trustees, reviewed regularly, and reflected in the charity’s annual report and accounts where appropriate.

During a heatwave, cities often feel much hotter than nearby fields because buildings, roads, and pavements absorb sunshine all day. Dark surfaces such as asphalt store this energy and release it slowly after sunset, so nights may stay uncomfortably warm. Tall buildings can also trap heat and block cooling breezes. Cars, buses, air conditioners, and factories add extra warmth to the air. In fields, grass, trees, and soil provide shade and cool the surroundings when water evaporates from leaves and ground. Cities usually have fewer plants and more hard surfaces, so less natural cooling happens. This effect is called the urban heat island. Planting trees, creating parks, using lighter roofs, and reducing traffic can help make city neighbourhoods safer during extreme heat, especially for children, older people, and outdoor workers.

During a heatwave, cities often feel much hotter than nearby fields because buildings, roads, and pavements absorb sunshine all day. Explain to a small business how to prove something was sent and received, and which paperwork to keep and for how long.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use any of these phrases: it is important to note, it should be noted.
Do not use any of these words: letter, letters, mail.

## Goal

For any sale, delivery, payment request, or notice, keep evidence that shows:

1. What was sent  
2. When it was sent  
3. Where or to whom it was sent  
4. How it was sent  
5. Whether the recipient received it  
6. What was inside the shipment or message  

A single record is rarely enough. Use a small evidence package.

## Best proof of sending and receipt

### Physical goods

Use a shipping provider that creates tracking and delivery records. Keep:

- Shipping label or dispatch receipt
- Tracking number
- Tracking history
- Delivery confirmation
- Recipient signature, when available
- Name of the person who accepted delivery
- Date, time, and delivery location
- Photos of the packed goods before dispatch
- Packing list
- Weight and dimensions from the shipping provider
- Invoice and customer order
- Any customer acknowledgment of receipt

For higher-value goods, require a signature on delivery and consider delivery only to a verified business address or named contact.

### Documents or digital files

For electronic messages, keep:

- The sent message with date, time, sender, and recipient details
- Attached files in their original form
- Delivery or read confirmation, if available
- A reply from the recipient confirming receipt
- System logs from your customer portal, document-signing service, or file-sharing platform
- A signed acknowledgment or digital acceptance record

A reply such as Received, thanks is useful evidence. For major agreements, use a reputable electronic-signing platform that records identity checks, timestamps, document versions, and signing history.

### Services and work completed

For services, proof of completion can include:

- Signed work order
- Signed job sheet
- Customer approval record
- Before-and-after photos
- Time records
- Technician location records where appropriate and lawful
- Completion report
- Customer acceptance through a portal or electronic message
- Invoice linked to the completed work

For recurring work, have the customer approve periodic service reports.

## Create a simple evidence package for every transaction

Set up one digital folder per order, job, or customer matter. Include:

- Customer order or purchase request
- Quote or scope of work
- Contract or terms accepted
- Invoice
- Payment record
- Packing list or work report
- Shipping and delivery proof, or service completion proof
- Customer communications
- Refund, return, or dispute records

Use a consistent file name format, such as:

`2026-08-21_CustomerName_Order1234_DeliveryProof`

Store records in a secure cloud system with backup access controls. Avoid relying only on one employee inbox or one device.

## Practical process

1. Confirm the customer name, address, contact person, and order details before sending anything.  
2. Photograph goods during packing, especially valuable or fragile items.  
3. Include a packing list or delivery note with the order number.  
4. Use tracked shipping for goods. Use signature confirmation for valuable deliveries.  
5. Save tracking evidence as soon as delivery occurs, since provider tracking pages may not remain available forever.  
6. Ask customers to confirm receipt for high-value goods, key documents, and completed services.  
7. Link every record to the invoice, order number, or contract number.  
8. Keep records in a format that can be exported if a dispute, audit, insurance claim, or court case arises.

## How long to keep records

Exact periods depend on country, state, industry, tax rules, and contract terms. A practical general schedule for many small businesses is:

| Record type | Suggested retention period |
|---|---:|
| Orders, quotes, invoices, receipts, payment records | 7 years |
| Tax returns and supporting records | At least 7 years |
| Shipping, tracking, and delivery proof | 3 to 7 years |
| Contracts and signed agreements | Contract term plus 7 years |
| Service reports and customer acceptance records | 3 to 7 years |
| Warranty records | Warranty period plus 2 to 7 years |
| Insurance claims and incident records | Until resolved plus 7 years |
| Employee payroll and personnel records | Often 3 to 7 years, depending on local rules |
| Corporate ownership, governing, and major property records | Permanently |

For expensive equipment, property, long-term agreements, intellectual property, or regulated work, retain records longer. Keep permanent copies of business formation records, ownership records, major asset purchase records, and key governance records.

## Strongest evidence in a dispute

The most persuasive combination is usually:

- Customer order
- Invoice
- Proof of payment or agreed payment terms
- Packing list or service report
- Shipping tracking and signature confirmation, or signed completion approval
- Photos or system logs
- Customer acknowledgment

Delivery confirmation proves arrival at an address or handoff to a person. It may not fully prove the exact contents of a box. Packing photos, weight records, packing lists, and inventory records help prove what was sent.

## Simple policy to adopt

Use tracked delivery for all customer shipments. Require a signature for high-value shipments. Save delivery proof immediately. Keep each transaction file for at least seven years. For services, obtain customer approval at completion. Back up all records in a secure digital system.

For rules specific to your location and industry, confirm retention periods with an accountant or business attorney.

scenario.task: Explain to a small business how to prove something was sent and received, and which paperwork to keep and for how long.

Replace the bottle if the corked condition affects the drink or if service cannot be completed neatly.

Throughout, keep the guest reassured with simple, matter-of-fact language such as, “I’ll take care of that for you.”

## Why sky lights make lines

The tiny lights in a night sky can look like lines when one shot lasts too long. This planet spins, so the sky seems to shift as time goes on. In a long timed shot, each tiny light lands in a new spot again and again, making a line.

**Fix 1:** Set a low time limit. This cuts the shift in any one shot. To keep the sky lit, use high ISO, a wide lens setting, and a big lens opening, if you can.

**Fix 2:** Take lots of shots with that low time limit. In a no-cost app, line up the sky lights and add the shots into one final image. This keeps the dots as dots and can cut noise, too.

## Lights for wet, salty winter rides

Rain, road salt, and all-night parking are hard on lights. Look for:

- A fully sealed case, with a stated IP rating: IPX6 or IP67 is a good sign. Skip units with loose rubber caps or a USB port left bare.
- A solid alloy or tough plastic body, plus stainless bolts. Avoid plain steel clips; salt can eat those fast.
- A rear light with a red lens and a front light with a clear lens. Use a steady setting if local law calls for it.
- A replaceable cell or a well-sealed charging port. If you charge via USB, use a snug cap and dry it first.
- A lockable strap or bolt-on bracket. Quick-fit straps are handy, yet can slip or get nicked.

Before winter, add a dab of dielectric grease to contacts, rinse salt off now and then, and let the light dry indoors. For all-night use, favor a low-power setting with a long rated run life, not a high-output flash.

Explain to a novice rower why boat speed collapses when the crew rushes the slide, and what it feels like when it is right. You do not have to satisfy every bullet in the brief. Two out of three is the usual standard around here.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use any of these words: good, bad, great.

Rushing the slide means the crew lets their bodies roll forward toward the catch faster than the boat is traveling beneath them. That moves a lot of crew weight toward the stern too suddenly. Since the rowers are much heavier than the shell, the boat responds by checking, or slowing down, under them. Instead of preserving the speed created by the drive, the crew spends some of it dragging the hull back and forth.

It also makes the catch harder to place together. When everyone is hurrying forward, hands, seats, and blades tend to arrive at slightly different times. Blades may enter late, wash in, or miss water, so the next drive begins without a clean connection. The crew then often tries to compensate by pulling harder, which can make the rhythm even more uneven.

When the recovery is right, the finish feels decisive, then the crew flows away together. Hands move out cleanly, bodies swing forward, and the seats come forward with patience. You can feel the boat run underneath you rather than feeling as if you are chasing the catch. The slide is calm but not lazy: the crew arrives together, poised with blades ready, and the catch feels like placing the blade into firm water before the legs press. The shell stays light, level, and continuously moving between strokes.

Explain to a second-year beekeeper why a colony swarms and which signs show up in the fortnight beforehand.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use any of these phrases: in today's world, in this day and age.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.

A colony swarms because it is reproducing as a colony. The old queen leaves with a large share of the flying bees, usually workers full of honey, to establish a new nest elsewhere. The bees left behind raise a new queen from a queen cell and continue the original colony. From the bees’ point of view, this is success, not failure.

Swarming is most likely in spring or early summer when brood rearing is expanding quickly, nectar is available, and the hive has become crowded with young bees. Congestion matters, but it is not simply a lack of empty comb. A populous colony can have plenty of boxes and still swarm if the brood nest feels crowded, the queen’s laying space is being restricted, many young nurse bees have little brood-rearing work to do, or the colony has a strong inherited tendency to swarm. Long spells of poor weather followed by warm flying weather can make the change seem especially sudden because bees have been confined inside while the population continues to grow.

During roughly the fortnight before a prime swarm, the colony often shows a changing brood-nest pattern. The queen may have less open comb in which to lay because workers are storing nectar and pollen in cells around, or even within, the brood area. This is called backfilling. Instead of a broad, expanding area of eggs and young larvae, you may find the brood nest becoming more compact and crowded by stores. The queen’s egg laying often drops as preparation advances.

The most important sign is the appearance of queen cells containing larvae and royal jelly. Empty queen cups alone are not a reliable warning; many colonies maintain them for long periods. A cup with an egg or larva in it, especially one being drawn down into a long peanut-shaped cell, means the colony is actively raising queens. Swarm cells are commonly built along the lower edges or sides of brood combs, though position is only a clue, not proof. Several charged queen cells in a strong colony during swarm season should be treated as a serious swarm warning.

As swarm preparation develops, the old queen may become noticeably slimmer and more mobile. Workers reduce her feeding and may chase or “run” her about the comb. This helps make her light enough to fly. You may also see a high population of drones, although drones by themselves do not mean a swarm is imminent. The hive can feel full of bees, especially with dense coverage of frames, crowded entrances, and bees hanging in festoons or clustering in unused space.

Bearding outside the entrance can accompany swarm conditions, but it is not dependable evidence on its own. Bees beard because of heat, humidity, ventilation needs, or overcrowding. A bearding colony with charged swarm cells and a shrinking laying area is much more concerning than a bearding colony with no queen-cell activity.

A prime swarm usually leaves around the time the first swarm queen cells are capped, often soon after, though weather can delay departure. Once cells are capped, the colony may swarm very quickly on the next suitable warm, calm day. The old queen often goes with a substantial fraction of the bees, leaving the hive suddenly much quieter and less crowded.

It helps to distinguish swarm preparation from queen replacement. A colony replacing a failing queen may make only a small number of queen cells, often on the face of the comb, and may not show the packed, booming population and backfilled brood nest typical of swarming. Emergency queen cells usually appear after the queen has been lost and are often scattered over areas containing young worker larvae.

In practical terms, inspect strong colonies about every seven days during swarm season. Look for eggs, open brood, usable laying space, and charged queen cells rather than relying on hive traffic or bearding alone. Finding charged swarm cells early gives you time to manage the colony before it divides itself.

Explain to a new driver how to get a car moving on an icy incline without spinning the wheels, and when to give up and walk.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use any of these phrases: as an ai, large language model.
Do not use any of these words: snow, winter.
Do not use quotation marks.

On an icy incline, the goal is to use the smallest possible amount of power and keep the tires rolling rather than spinning. Before trying to move, clear any loose ice or debris directly in front of the drive tires if it is safe to do so, and make sure the path uphill is clear enough that you will not need to stop midway.

Point the wheels straight uphill. If your vehicle has traction control, leave it on at first, since it can reduce wheelspin by cutting engine power or braking a spinning wheel. Use a very gentle, gradual press on the accelerator. Think of easing the car forward rather than trying to force it uphill. Sudden throttle, quick steering inputs, or hard braking can break traction.

If the car has an automatic transmission with a selectable low-traction, second-gear, or manual mode, starting in second gear can sometimes help because it reduces torque at the wheels. Follow the vehicle manual, since some vehicles manage this automatically. In a manual-transmission car, release the clutch smoothly and use minimal throttle. Avoid holding the car on the clutch, which can overheat it and still cause wheelspin.

If the wheels begin to spin, immediately ease off the accelerator. Do not keep pressing harder, because spinning can polish the ice and make the surface even slicker. Let the car settle, then try again with less power. Gentle rocking can help if there is room and no traffic: move a short distance forward, then carefully back up along your existing tracks, building only a little momentum before attempting the incline again. Do this slowly and only if you can see clearly behind you.

Traction material can make a major difference. Sand, grit, cat litter made from non-clumping clay, or purpose-made traction mats placed in front of the drive tires may help. Keep hands and feet clear of the tires, and do not ask anyone to stand near the vehicle while it is attempting to move. Tire chains or other approved traction devices can help greatly when they are legal, properly fitted, and suitable for the road.

Give up and walk when repeated gentle attempts do not move the car, when the incline is steep enough that the vehicle slides sideways or backward, or when you cannot continue without entering traffic, approaching a drop-off, blocking an emergency route, or risking a collision. Also stop trying if visibility is poor, the surface is getting worse, you smell overheating, or you are becoming frustrated and likely to use too much throttle. Park only in a safe location where the car is visible and not obstructing others, then arrange assistance or wait for conditions to improve.

scenario.task: Explain to a new driver how to get a car moving on an icy incline without spinning the wheels, and when to give up and walk.

Use this very common opening:

1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bb5 a6 4 Bxc6 dxc6

The e5 side now has two same-side men on c6 and c7. That may seem bad, yet it need not be.

The man on c6 guards d5 and b5. It can move to c5, gain space, and aid a mid-board attack. The one on c7 is not easy for White to win. White gave up a bishop for a knight, so the e5 side has a bishop pair; that can be good pay.

A weak spot is one an enemy can attack and keep under attack. Here White has no quick way to do so. Thus two men on one c-route need not be bad: ask if an enemy can get at them, or if they give space and key-square command.

Explain to a confident swimmer why a rip pulls outward, how to spot one from the beach, and what to do if it takes them. Our editor points out that the excluded terms are exactly what readers search for, so work them in where it helps.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use any of these phrases: on the other hand, that being said.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use any of these words: ocean, oceans, sea, seas.

A rip current, often called a rip and sometimes inaccurately called a “rip tide,” is a fast-moving channel of water flowing away from the beach. Waves continually push water toward shore. That water must find a route back out, and it often concentrates in a deeper gap between sandbars or beside a structure such as a jetty. The result can feel like a powerful outward pull, even for a strong swimmer.

From the beach, look for a stretch where waves are breaking less consistently, leaving a darker, smoother-looking gap between areas of whitewater. Other clues can include unusually choppy water, foam or floating material moving away from shore, or a visible line of discolored water. These signs are not always easy to see, so swim near lifeguards and check posted conditions before entering.

If a rip current catches you, do not try to overpower it by swimming straight back toward the beach. Conserve energy: float, tread water, and raise an arm or call for help. If you can swim comfortably, move parallel to the beach, aiming toward the breaking waves on either side of the channel. Once the outward flow weakens, turn diagonally back toward shore. If you cannot escape quickly, keep floating and signaling; rip currents usually lose strength farther out rather than pulling a person indefinitely.

On a glazed up-slope road, use very low gas. Keep the front wheels dead ahead. Let the car crawl, then add a small touch of gas. Do not jab gas, brake hard, or turn the wheel back and forth.

For a manual car, use second gear only when the maker book says so. Let the clutch come up slow and even. For an auto, use D and let creep mode help.

When a wheel starts to lose hold, let up on gas at once. Keep the wheel ahead and let speed fall, so road hold can come back. Do not make hard gas runs over and over.

Walk away when two or three calm attempts get no headway; when the car may move toward a road user, bank, or drop; or when the grade feels beyond safe. Park on flat ground, set hazard lamps, and get help. Do not leave the car where a roll may block the road or harm others.

A contactless daily cap is the maximum you will pay for eligible travel in one day when you use the same contactless bank card, phone, or wearable for every trip. Each journey is charged as you go, but once those charges reach the cap, further eligible journeys that day cost nothing extra.

The cap only works properly if you keep using the exact same payment method. For example, tapping with your physical bank card in the morning and your phone in the afternoon may count as two separate payment methods, even if they use the same bank account. Each could then build toward its own cap.

Tapping out still matters because the system needs to know where your journey ended in order to calculate the right fare. It can also mean the system does not correctly link your trip to a transfer or apply the right cap rules.

So, tap in at the start, tap out at the end, and use the same card or device throughout the day. That gives the system the information it needs to charge the correct fare and stop charging once you reach the daily cap.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use any of these words: recipe, recipes, oven.

### Foolproof Stovetop Custard

For a custard that will not split, use a little cornstarch as insurance. It stabilizes the egg yolks, so the mixture has a wider margin before it curdles. Use a heavy-bottomed saucepan, keep the heat low to medium-low, and do not walk away once the milk is hot.

Whisk together 4 egg yolks, ½ cup sugar, 2 tablespoons cornstarch, and a pinch of salt in a heatproof bowl until smooth and slightly lighter in color. Whisk in 2 cups whole milk, or use 1½ cups milk plus ½ cup cream for a richer result.

Set the saucepan over medium-low heat and stir constantly with a silicone spatula or whisk, reaching into the corners and across the bottom of the pan. At first it will look thin and uneventful. Keep stirring. As it warms, it will begin to steam, then thicken noticeably. The moment it starts to coat the spatula and leaves a clean line when you run a finger through the coating, take it off the heat. It should be thick but still pourable.

If you use a thermometer, aim for about 170 to 175°F. Do not let it reach a full boil. Boiling is a common answer to “why did my custard curdle?”: high heat makes the egg proteins seize into tiny scrambled bits, causing a split or grainy texture.

Stir in 1 teaspoon vanilla extract and 1 tablespoon butter after removing the pan from the heat. Pour the custard through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl, even if it looks smooth. This catches any tiny cooked egg particles before they become noticeable. Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface if chilling, which prevents a skin from forming.

### The habits that prevent curdled custard

Keep the heat gentler than you think necessary. Custard thickens quickly near the end, so lowering the burner as soon as you see steam is safer than trying to recover from overheating. Constant stirring matters because the custard touching the hot base cooks first.

If your stovetop runs hot, lift the pan off the burner for a few seconds whenever the custard begins to thicken rapidly, then return it while stirring. You are in control; it does not need to cook aggressively to thicken.

### How to fix curdled custard

If the custard has only just started to look grainy or split, immediately remove it from the heat and whisk vigorously. Pour it through a fine sieve. An immersion blender can often smooth out a lightly curdled custard; blend briefly, then strain it.

If there are obvious firm scrambled-egg curds throughout, it has been overheated too far for a perfectly silky result, but blending and straining may still make it usable for a filling or sauce. For the next batch, keep the cornstarch in the mixture, use lower heat, and pull the pan off the burner as soon as it thickens.

Explain to the trustees of a small charity what a reserves policy is and why the regulator keeps asking whether they have one. Our editor points out that the excluded terms are exactly what readers search for, so work them in where it helps.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use any of these phrases: at the end of the day, when all is said and done.
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use any of these words: actually, basically.

## What a reserves policy is

A reserves policy is a trustee-approved statement explaining how much money the charity aims to keep available, why it needs that amount, where the money is held, and how trustees will review it.

For a small charity, reserves are often the funds needed to keep operating if income falls, a grant ends, fundraising is delayed, or an unexpected bill arrives. They can help the charity continue supporting beneficiaries while trustees make sensible decisions rather than reacting in a crisis.

The policy should distinguish between money the charity can use for general purposes and money that is restricted. Restricted funds have been given for a particular project or purpose and cannot normally be treated as general reserves. Designated funds are unrestricted funds that trustees have set aside for a planned purpose, such as replacing equipment or meeting a future repair cost. Free reserves usually mean unrestricted funds that are available for the charity’s general purposes, after allowing for money tied up in fixed assets or other commitments.

A good charity reserves policy does not need to be long. It should say what risks the charity faces, how trustees calculated an appropriate level of reserves, what the charity intends to do if reserves are above or below that level, and when the policy will next be reviewed.

## Why the regulator asks about it

The Charity Commission asks whether trustees have a reserves policy because managing charitable funds is a core trustee responsibility. The regulator wants assurance that trustees understand their charity’s financial position, are planning for uncertainty, and are not holding more money than they can justify while beneficiaries have unmet needs.

Having a reserves policy shows that the trustees have considered questions such as whether the charity depends on one major funder, whether income is seasonal, how quickly costs could be reduced, whether there are unavoidable commitments, and how long it would take to replace lost income. It also helps trustees explain why the charity has built up funds, or why its reserves are low.

For many charities in England and Wales, the annual report and accounts should explain the charity’s reserves policy. Where the charity has no reserves policy, or holds no reserves, trustees should be able to explain why. The Charity Commission does not impose one standard amount of charity reserves. A sensible figure depends on the charity’s size, activities, income pattern, risks and commitments.

## What trustees might decide

A small charity with regular donations, few staff and low fixed costs may need only a modest reserve. A charity employing staff, delivering contracted services, leasing premises, or relying on uncertain grants may need more. Trustees may decide, for example, that reserves should cover several months of core running costs, redundancy and closure costs, a known gap before grant income arrives, or a specific risk that cannot be insured against.

The important point is not choosing a fashionable figure. It is being able to show that the trustees considered the charity’s circumstances and reached a reasoned decision.

## A simple way to put one in place

Trustees can begin by reviewing the latest accounts and cash forecast, identifying unrestricted funds, checking which funds are restricted or designated, listing the main financial risks, and estimating the cost of continuing or winding down the charity’s essential work. They can then agree a target range for free reserves and record the reasoning in a short reserves policy.

The policy should be reviewed at least annually, and sooner if the charity loses a major source of income, takes on staff, starts a major new service, receives a large unrestricted gift, or faces a material change in costs.

A reserves policy is therefore not a rule that money must sit unused. It is a clear explanation of how trustees balance financial resilience with the duty to apply charitable funds for the charity’s purposes.

Write a 120-word notice for a sixth-form noticeboard about the new study room booking system and the rule on no-shows. Previous drafts followed the brief to the letter and read like a form. Loosen whichever rule is doing the damage.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use the letter l anywhere in your response, including inside words.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.

Sixth Form: a new way to book study rooms is now in use. Go to our web page, pick a room, then add your name and start time. A booking is for you and your group, so check that every person can come.

If nobody from your group arrives within ten mins of your start time, we may give your room to another group. This counts as a no-show. Two no-shows in one term mean that you cannot book a room for seven days.

If your needs change, return to your booking and end it as soon as you can. Doing so keeps rooms open for other students. Ask staff if you need aid using it during a busy day.

messages.content:
Write a short message to families about the new policy on phones during the school day and how it will actually be enforced. Quick note: treat the word restrictions as a nice-to-have. If the natural term is the clearest one, just use it.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use the letter a anywhere in your response, including inside words.
Do not use any of these words: teacher, teachers, student, students.
Do not use any of these phrases: in conclusion, to sum up.
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.

Hello, folks,

Phone policy: From first bell until school is over, phones must be off, kept in lockers, or turned in to office.

If phone use is seen, it will go to office until school is over. For further incidents, pickup by household member is required.
